title: Redistricting agonistes
summary: Sen. Arthur Ellis' quixotic, one-man campaign to force a Senate vote on a redistricting bill is not likely to succeed, writes Josh Kurtz, but it's a credit to Ellis and it illustrates the political and social dynamics at work in the State House.
content:
by Josh Kurtz, Maryland Matters February 22, 2026

by Josh Kurtz, Maryland Matters February 22, 2026

In the clubby, go-along-to-get-along world of Annapolis, Sen. Arthur Ellis (D-Charles) is seen as something of an odd duck.

He’s not a team player. He goes off on tangents sometimes and wages quixotic battles, often in opposition to fellow Democrats.

He’s unabashedly liberal and impatient, in a Senate Democratic caucus that remains, even in this blue state in 2026, moderate and politically cautious.

A lot of Annapolis power players still keep their distance. Almost eight years ago, Ellis knocked off powerful Senate Finance Chair Thomas “Mac” Middleton, a popular figure among political insiders, in a hard-fought and racially tinged Democratic primary.

Ellis is not a regular participant in the 90-night Annapolis Bacchanalia of the legislative session.

But say this for Ellis: He’s got guts.

If the challenge to Middleton wasn’t enough proof, consider Ellis’ one-man protest against Senate President Bill Ferguson’s refusal to bring congressional redistricting legislation to the floor. It’s one of several story lines in Annapolis as policymakers continue to wrestle with what to do – or not do.

The battles have become increasingly personal, not just tactical, with long-term political and relational implications, as Gov. Wes Moore (D) and House Democratic leaders stand on one side and Ferguson and his lieutenants stand on the other. National Democratic pooh-bahs, for better or worse, are watching.

But really, the impasse serves as a reminder of the political dynamics and the social dynamics in the State House.

Ellis said earlier this month he would not answer quorum calls on the Senate floor as long as the redistricting bill languishes in the Rules Committee. Merely symbolic, perhaps. But gutsy just the same.

Old Annapolis hands continue to shake their heads at Ellis’ tactics. He is an imperfect messenger, and given the way things work in the capital, he probably wound up undermining his own position – even if his message was pretty potent.

He isn’t the only Senate Democrat who has publicly called for Maryland to redraw its congressional boundaries right away. Sen. Clarence K. Lam (D-Howard and Anne Arundel) said last year he’d sponsor a redistricting bill this session; in response, Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) forced him out as chair of the Senate Executive Nominations Committee.

Lam’s fellow Democrats took notice. So now – with the exception of Ellis – no Democratic senators, regardless of their true feelings, are publicly contradicting their leader. Lam continues to say he wants new maps, but his remarks haven’t been as personal or as pointed as Ellis’.

In a chamber where Democrats hold a 34-13 advantage, where every Democrat but one seems like very safe bets for reelection in the fall, how can they be so cool to middecade redistricting? In the House of Delegates, 98 of 99 Democrats who were present when the redistricting bill came up late last month voted yes. Do senators really feel so differently from their colleagues across the hall?

It strains credulity to think that they do. But their silence is also perfectly explicable.

Ferguson has made it clear that he won’t move the redistricting bill, and he has his reasons. Middecade redistricting, propelled by President Donald Trump and Texas Republicans, is morally wrong and legally and politically risky for Democrats, Ferguson argues. Retaliating against the GOP is not high on any constituent’s wish list, he says, and with the candidate filing deadline on Tuesday, it’s logistically impossible.

These are not insignificant points, and yet they seem to be at odds with the energy and sentiments of many Democratic activists. Still, Ferguson gave redistricting yet another eulogy during a news conference on Friday.

Who were Senate Democratic senators going to side with? Lam, already disciplined for his heresies and something of a scold in his colleagues’ minds? The frequently isolated Ellis? Or Ferguson, who holds all the political power in the chamber, who hands out plum assignments and determines the fate of every single piece of legislation?

The hush speaks volumes.

It was positively surreal, during Moore’s recent State of the State address, to see senators sitting on their hands when the governor called for a vote on redistricting. It was like a State of the Union speech when the members of Congress not in the president’s party sit mute. Only this time the stony silence came from the governor’s own party, in the House chambers where members had recently passed the redistricting plan. Weird.

So the redistricting bill will languish in the Senate Rules Committee and then die.

Ferguson, of course, will be culpable. But so will Moore: Consider this another example of the governor talking big and then not fully delivering, succumbing to the whims and ways and wiles of the legislature without a focused campaign to bring lawmakers to his side. National media outlets like Politico and Axios are starting to take notice.

Moore has made strong arguments for a redistricting vote – in national interviews. His redistricting commission, which was designed to anchor and augment the push for a new map, was put together hastily and operated largely in obscurity, sometimes behind closed doors.

This was no way to marshal a campaign at home in Maryland, where redistricting needed buy-in not just from state lawmakers but from party activists, in-state opinion leaders and even everyday voters. But the plan never really reached the public’s radar – and pressure from U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and former U.S. Attorney General Eric Holder and Moore’s ongoing national media tour was unlikely to sway Ferguson and his devoted followers in the Maryland Senate.

Will there be any political peril in the primaries for Democratic senators who let re-redistricting die? Where are the angry party activists expressing outrage?

Will Moore activate his political slate to go after any senators who oppose him on redistricting? Will these senators ever fully explain why they’re passing on an opportunity to take on Trump directly and level the national congressional playing field – and quite possibly end the political career of U.S. Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st)?

With just hours before the candidate filing deadline, it sure doesn’t seem like there will be any political ramifications for the recalcitrant senators. Ellis has announced he is abandoning Annapolis for a congressional bid this year.

As of Sunday, only half a dozen Democratic incumbents had primary challengers of varying quality and potential (Ferguson is one of them). Is there a groundswell of opposition about to emerge? Probably not.

Since Ellis launched his personal protest, some veteran Annapolis observers have posited that Ferguson’s legendary predecessor, the late Senate President Thomas V. Mike Miller Jr. (D), would never have tolerated such visible and vocal dissent.

I’m not sure that’s true. And I also have to imagine that Miller – who lived for 12 years with Harris as a burr in his side – would be fully in favor of an 8-0 map. And he might be wondering why Maryland’s Senate Democrats have chosen to remain on the sidelines during this very consequential nationwide fight.
